\chapter{Describing Things}
\label{ch:sa-describing-things}
\hlchaptermodality{15}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at something in Sanskrit and ask who or where it is — and I can say what the six words have in common.}

Say the near word, the far word and the question word in a row, and name the part that changed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mahat]{\sk{महत्} (mahat) — big}

\label{lesson:SA-C15-big}



\begin{quote}
You can already name things. This is how you POINT at them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{महत्}}
\textbf{\sk{महत्}} — \emph{mahat} — big.

Put it in front of a word you already know and you have said something new. That is all an adjective does in this language.

The last lesson of this chapter gives the one rule that governs every adjective you will ever meet here.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\sk{महत्}\textquotedblright{} three times, pointing at something different each time
  \item it once with a word you already know after it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{mahat}? (\textbf{big}.) Where does it go — before the word it describes, or after? (\textbf{Before.})
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[ba]{\sk{ब} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S216-letter-ba}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ल} · \sk{◌ो} · \sk{थ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ब}}
\textbf{\sk{ब}} — \emph{ba}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{b}, it is \textbf{ba}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a counterclockwise oval body
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item a down-right inner diagonal
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ब} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{कुटुम्बम्}} \emph{kuṭumbam} — family, household — a word Sanskrit itself borrowed, before other languages borrowed it back
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ब}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the body's upper-right junction and circle counterclockwise around the oval to its lower-right junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift at the body's upper-left interior and draw the inner diagonal down-right
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified four-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the oval differently
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: JackPotte, ‘Devanagari b \sk{ब}.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 29 March 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ब} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{कुटुम्बम्}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ब} three times, saying \emph{ba} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ब} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ब}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ba}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[u]{\sk{उ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S121-letter-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌ो} · \sk{थ} · \sk{ब}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{उ}}
\textbf{\sk{उ}} — \emph{u}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel}: the full-size letter a vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. Inside a word the same vowel is written as a small sign instead.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined upper bowl and lower loop
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{उ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{उत्तम}} \emph{uttama} — good
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{उ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the headline junction, curve down and left around the upper bowl, then sweep back through the waist and around the lower loop without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The pen comes up 1 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified modern printed teaching form; everyday handwriting may simplify the curves
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{उ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{उ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{उत्तम}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{उ} three times, saying \emph{u} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{उ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}

\section[before the noun, and it AGREES]{before the noun, and it AGREES — five words, one rule}

\label{lesson:SA-C15-adjective-system}



\begin{quote}
Say the five words from this chapter out loud, then say each one in front of a noun you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: where an adjective goes}]
You did not learn five separate words. You learned \textbf{where an adjective goes}, and five words that go there.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
big & \textbf{\sk{महत्}} \emph{mahat} \\
small & \textbf{\sk{अल्प}} \emph{alpa} \\
good & \textbf{\sk{उत्तम}} \emph{uttama} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Sanskrit agrees too, and in more ways than Hindi does — this is where Hindi's habit comes from.

This is worth more than the five words are. Every noun you already know — your name, the house, the water, the day — can now take any of them in front, and every adjective you meet from here goes in the same place.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} each of the five in front of a noun you already know
  \item \emph{Say it:} two of them with the same noun, one after the other
  \item \emph{Notice:} whether the adjective changed shape when the noun did
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does an adjective go in this language? (\textbf{In front of the noun.}) Does it change shape to match the noun? (and it AGREES.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṣa]{\sk{ष} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S118-letter-ssa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{थ} · \sk{ब} · \sk{उ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ष}}
\textbf{\sk{ष}} — \emph{ṣa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṣ}, it is \textbf{ṣa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a U-shaped body drawn from the left side around the lower bowl and up the right side
  \item a retraced top-to-bottom right stem
  \item a down-right inner diagonal
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ष} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{क्षीरम्}} \emph{kṣīram} — milk — an origin scholars still argue over, and the dessert word it left behind
  \item \textbf{\sk{अक्षि}} \emph{akṣi} — eye — unbroken from Sanskrit to English, and the reason eyes get their own grammatical number
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ष}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the left side, curve counterclockwise around the lower bowl, and rise along the right side to the headline without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom, retracing its upper body-side segment before continuing below the bowl
  \item \textbf{3.} lift at the upper-left interior and draw the inner diagonal down-right to the bowl junction
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified four-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ष}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{ष} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{क्षीरम्}  ·  \sk{अक्षि}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ष} three times, saying \emph{ṣa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ष} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ष}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṣa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[au]{\sk{◌ौ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S115-vowel-sign-au}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ब} · \sk{उ} · \sk{ष}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ौ}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ौ}} — \emph{au}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: the ā bar plus a double stroke above.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{न}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ौ}} = \textbf{\sk{नौ}} — \emph{nau}.

No word in this book has put \sk{◌ौ} in front of you yet, and that is worth saying plainly rather than hiding: this one is here because it is built from two shapes you already know, and because the running text of later chapters uses it.

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ौ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ौ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{◌ौ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{◌ौ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ौ} three times, saying \emph{au} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ौ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ौ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{au} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
